issues.title_en: Indonesia battles Mount Bromo wildfire as El Nino takes root
issues.summary:
Malang, Indonesia: Indonesian authorities battled Friday to contain a wildfire that has swept through Mount Bromo National Park on Java island, destroying more than 120 hectares as the country braces itself for an extreme El Nino-fuelled dry season.

The fire started Monday near Mount Bromo in East Java, one of Indonesia's most visited tourist destinations but now closed until further notice.

Local authorities deployed two water-bombing helicopters against the flames that have razed at least 127 hectares of national park land to date, fire official Bambang Setyo Antoko told AFP.

The destroyed area is equivalent to about 180 soccer fields.

"We're very dependent on wind conditions," Bambang said of the firefighting effort ahead.

National park official Rudijanta Tjahja Nugraha said the area on fire was in a steep, cliffside region, making it difficult for firefighters to reach.

It was not known how the fire started, but Bambang said the park was extremely dry as El Nino conditions take root in Indonesia.

Mount Bromo, famed for its volcanic scenery, previously caught fire in 2023.

That blaze broke out when a couple lit a flare during a pre-wedding photo shoot and destroyed more than 500 hectares of land.

Indonesia's BMKG weather agency has warned that the 2026 dry season will be more intense and prolonged than usual, with a higher risk for wildfires and drought due in part to El Nino.

According to the Ministry of Forestry, more than 107,000 hectares of land burned in Indonesia between January and June this year -- more than double the area destroyed in forest fires in 2023.

The last El Nino helped make 2023 and 2024 the two hottest years globally on record.

El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns.

In India and Southeast Asia, it typically causes drier conditions.

issues.title_en: Malaysia Airlines to test all pilots after Indonesia drug arrest
issues.summary:
Kuala Lumpur: Malaysia Airlines' parent firm announced on Friday mandatory drug screenings for its pilots, after one of them tested positive for a cocktail of narcotics and was arrested in Indonesia for smuggling.

Authorities at Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport arrested the 39-year-old pilot last month, shortly after arriving from Kuala Lumpur, for allegedly attempting to smuggle more than 70,000 ecstasy tablets in his suitcase.

Malaysia Aviation Group said in a statement on Friday that it would carry out tests "for all active pilots, beyond industry practice".

The group, which also owns budget airline Firefly, said the process would begin with 1,260 pilots from the national carrier, with tests to be completed by August 15.

Pilots who are not tested will "not operate flights" until they have been cleared, the company said.

The process would complement the aviation group's "existing random testing programme", it added.

"Operational safety and crew fitness for duty are non-negotiable," said the group's president and chief executive, Captain Nasaruddin A. Bakar.

"We take any breach of our safety standards seriously and have acted swiftly to enhance mandatory drug screening across our active pilots."

The detained pilot faces the death penalty on conviction in Indonesia.

Results of his urine test came back positive for meth, MDMA and cocaine, according to Indonesian customs officials.

Malaysia Aviation Group has said he was not the one who flew the plane from Kuala Lumpur that day, but a cockpit "observer" who had been "off duty for two days preceding the incident".

It added that the aircraft "was operated safely at all times by two qualified operating pilots".
